claim: The anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN) is an exclusive target of the hippocampus (HPC) within the medial hypothalamic defense system.
source: Here, using adult male mice, we show that the anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN) is best positioned to control this task as an exclusive target of the hippocampus (HPC) within the medial hypothalamic defense system.
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing experiments showing hippocampal axon terminals are found almost exclusively at the AHN, but not the PMD and VMHdm/c (Figure 3b and c).

claim: The HPC→AHN pathway mediates the contextual memory of predator threats.
source: Selective optogenetic stimulation and inhibition of hippocampal inputs to the AHN revealed that the HPC→AHN pathway not only mediates the contextual memory of predator threats but also controls the goal-directed escape by transmitting information about the surrounding environment.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments showing that mice failed to remember and avoid L-Felinine context when the HPC→AHN pathway was inhibited (Figure 6c and d).

claim: The HPC→AHN pathway controls goal-directed escape by transmitting information about the surrounding environment.
source: Selective optogenetic stimulation and inhibition of hippocampal inputs to the AHN revealed that the HPC→AHN pathway not only mediates the contextual memory of predator threats but also controls the goal-directed escape by transmitting information about the surrounding environment.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing that pathway stimulation evoked goal-directed escapes toward shelter (Figure 7f–i), and inhibition experiments showing disrupted escape to shelter (Figure 8g–k).

claim: Innate defensive behaviors are generated by the medial hypothalamic defensive system.
source: Innate defensive behaviors are generated by the medial hypothalamic defensive system (Canteras, 2002), consisting of the anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN) (Fuchs et al., 1985; Lamontagne et al., 2016), the dorsomedial and central region of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHdm/c) Fuchs et al., 1985; Wang et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2016b; Pérez-Gómez et al., 2015 and the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMD) (Canteras, 2002; Canteras, 2008; Wang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on the medial hypothalamic defensive system.

claim: The medial hypothalamic defensive system consists of the anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN), the dorsomedial and central region of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHdm/c), and the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMD).
source: Innate defensive behaviors are generated by the medial hypothalamic defensive system (Canteras, 2002), consisting of the anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN) (Fuchs et al., 1985; Lamontagne et al., 2016), the dorsomedial and central region of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHdm/c) Fuchs et al., 1985; Wang et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2016b; Pérez-Gómez et al., 2015 and the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMD) (Canteras, 2002; Canteras, 2008; Wang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature defining the components of the medial hypothalamic defensive system.

claim: The three nuclei of the medial hypothalamic defensive system (AHN, VMHdm/c, PMD) are densely interconnected.
source: These three distinct nuclei are densely interconnected and become highly active upon predator exposure (Dielenberg et al., 2001; Blanchard et al., 2005; Martinez et al., 2008; Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020) to control motor outputs at the level of periaqueductal gray (PAG) (Evans et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Canteras and Goto, 1999; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature describing the connectivity of these nuclei.

claim: The three nuclei of the medial hypothalamic defensive system become highly active upon predator exposure.
source: These three distinct nuclei are densely interconnected and become highly active upon predator exposure (Dielenberg et al., 2001; Blanchard et al., 2005; Martinez et al., 2008; Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020) to control motor outputs at the level of periaqueductal gray (PAG) (Evans et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Canteras and Goto, 1999; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing activation of these nuclei during predator exposure.

claim: The medial hypothalamic defensive system controls motor outputs at the level of periaqueductal gray (PAG).
source: These three distinct nuclei are densely interconnected and become highly active upon predator exposure (Dielenberg et al., 2001; Blanchard et al., 2005; Martinez et al., 2008; Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020) to control motor outputs at the level of periaqueductal gray (PAG) (Evans et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Canteras and Goto, 1999; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature describing the downstream targets of the medial hypothalamic defensive system.

claim: The environmental context of a salient event is first encoded within the hippocampus (HPC) as the collective activity of place cells and time cells.
source: It is well-established that the environmental context of a salient event is first encoded within the hippocampus (HPC) as the collective activity of place cells and time cells (Gross and Canteras, 2012; Silva et al., 2016a; Maren et al., 2013; Pentkowski et al., 2006; Kjelstrup et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2013; Lisman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on hippocampal encoding of contextual information.

claim: During memory recall, contextual information serves as a potent retrieval cue by reinstating patterns of brain activity observed during the original experience.
source: Later during memory recall, the contextual information serves as a potent retrieval cue by reinstating patterns of brain activity observed during the original experience. (Aqrabawi and Kim, 2018; Mandairon et al., 2014; Gottfried et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on memory retrieval mechanisms.

claim: High-frequency (20 Hz) AHN stimulation induced robust behavioral responses including jumping, freezing, and running in the absence of overt predator threat.
source: We first examined the effects of low- and high-frequency (6 Hz and 20 Hz) stimulation and found that the high-frequency stimulation generated robust behavioral responses in the absence of any overt predator threat, including jumping, freezing, and running, whereas the low-frequency stimulation increased only freezing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses to different frequencies of AHN stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Low-frequency (6 Hz) AHN stimulation increased only freezing behavior.
source: We first examined the effects of low- and high-frequency (6 Hz and 20 Hz) stimulation and found that the high-frequency stimulation generated robust behavioral responses in the absence of any overt predator threat, including jumping, freezing, and running, whereas the low-frequency stimulation increased only freezing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses to different frequencies of AHN stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: In condition 1 (easy escape), AHN stimulation induced bursts of running with a short latency of 5 ± 1.29 s.
source: In condition 1, AHN stimulation induced bursts of running ( > 0.3 m/s) with a short latency (5 ± 1.29 s) (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing latency to running behavior during AHN stimulation.

claim: Five of six AHN-ChR2 mice escaped the test arena in condition 1 (easy escape).
source: After bouts of running, AHN-ChR2 mice, but not GFP-control mice, initiated multiple escape jumps which resulted in five of six AHN-ChR2 mice escaping the test arena.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing escape success rates in AHN-ChR2 mice.

claim: AHN-ChR2 mice had significant increases in speed of locomotion, freezing, and jumping compared to GFP controls in condition 1 (easy escape).
source: We quantified the light-induced behavioral effect as a normalized difference between baseline epoch (OFF, 2 min) and stimulation epoch (ON, 2 min) and found that AHN-ChR2 mice had significant increases in the speed of locomotion, freezing, and jumping (Figure 1e–g) compared to GFP controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing quantified behavioral changes during AHN stimulation (Figure 1e–g).

claim: In condition 2 (hard escape), no AHN-ChR2 mice escaped the test arena.
source: In condition 2 (hard), no AHN-ChR2 mice escaped the test arena, but escape attempts were maintained with increased running, freezing, and jumping compared to GFP controls (Figure 1h–j, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing escape success rates in condition 2.

claim: In condition 2 (hard escape), escape attempts were maintained with increased running, freezing, and jumping compared to GFP controls.
source: In condition 2 (hard), no AHN-ChR2 mice escaped the test arena, but escape attempts were maintained with increased running, freezing, and jumping compared to GFP controls (Figure 1h–j, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses in condition 2 (Figure 1h–j).

claim: In condition 3 (impossible escape), AHN-ChR2 mice displayed persistent escape-struggle movements throughout the test despite limited mobility and long duration of physical restraint.
source: In condition 3, animals were physically restrained and received AHN stimulation (10 s ON, 10 s OFF) for 30 min, during which escape struggle movements were visually inspected and monitored using a collar sensor with a pulse oximeter. Despite limited mobility and the long duration of physical restraint, AHN-ChR2 mice, but not GFP controls, displayed persistent escape-struggle movements throughout the test.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing struggle movements during physical restraint.

claim: AHN activity is sufficient to evoke escape-associated behavioral responses in the absence of overt predator cues.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate that AHN activity is sufficient to evoke escape-associated behavioral responses in the absence of overt predator cues.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses to AHN stimulation across multiple conditions.

claim: All AHN-ChR2 mice exhibited dramatic flight responses upon AHN activation, immediately leaving and avoiding the photostimulation chamber in the real-time place avoidance assay.
source: All AHN-ChR2 mice exhibited dramatic flight responses upon AHN activation, immediately leaving and avoiding the photostimulation chamber (Figure 2e, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses in the real-time place avoidance assay (Figure 2e).

claim: Both 6 and 20 Hz AHN stimulation induced significant avoidance of the photostimulation chamber in ChR2 animals.
source: While both 6 and 20 Hz stimulation induced significant avoidance of the photostimulation chamber in ChR2 animals, there was a frequency-dependent magnitude of aversion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing place avoidance at different stimulation frequencies.

claim: The 20 Hz AHN stimulation induced a greater mean aversion index (- 0.89) than the 6 Hz stimulation (–0.63) in the real-time place avoidance assay.
source: The 20 Hz stimulation induced a greater mean aversion index (- 0.89) than the 6 Hz stimulation (–0.63) (Figure 2f) with no difference in total distance travelled during the test (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing quantified aversion indices at different stimulation frequencies (Figure 2f).

claim: There was no difference in total distance travelled during the real-time place avoidance test between 6 and 20 Hz AHN stimulation.
source: The 20 Hz stimulation induced a greater mean aversion index (- 0.89) than the 6 Hz stimulation (–0.63) (Figure 2f) with no difference in total distance travelled during the test (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing distance travelled during the test (Figure 2g).

claim: Both 6 and 20 Hz AHN stimulation produced significant conditioned place aversions.
source: Both 6 and 20 Hz stimulation produced significant conditioned place aversions with the 20 Hz stimulation inducing a greater mean aversion index (- 0.53) than the 6 Hz stimulation (- 0.20).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing conditioned place aversion after AHN stimulation.

claim: The 20 Hz AHN stimulation induced a greater mean conditioned place aversion index (- 0.53) than the 6 Hz stimulation (- 0.20).
source: Both 6 and 20 Hz stimulation produced significant conditioned place aversions with the 20 Hz stimulation inducing a greater mean aversion index (- 0.53) than the 6 Hz stimulation (- 0.20).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing quantified conditioned place aversion indices.

claim: AHN activity carries negative emotional valence.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that AHN activity carries negative emotional valence and can serve as a stimulus for the formation of a conditioned place aversion memory.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing place avoidance and conditioned place aversion induced by AHN stimulation.

claim: AHN activity can serve as a stimulus for the formation of a conditioned place aversion memory.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that AHN activity carries negative emotional valence and can serve as a stimulus for the formation of a conditioned place aversion memory.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing conditioned place aversion after AHN stimulation.

claim: HPC infusions led to the expression of ChR2-eYFP in the ventral two-thirds of the HPC, with minimal spread into adjacent cortical structures such as the entorhinal cortex.
source: HPC infusions led to the expression of ChR2-eYFP in the ventral two-thirds of the HPC, with minimal spread into adjacent cortical structures such as the entorhinal cortex which does not project to the AHN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by histological data showing viral expression pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).

claim: The entorhinal cortex does not project to the AHN.
source: HPC infusions led to the expression of ChR2-eYFP in the ventral two-thirds of the HPC, with minimal spread into adjacent cortical structures such as the entorhinal cortex which does not project to the AHN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript, likely based on established knowledge or tracing data.

claim: GFP-positive axon terminals from HPC were detected in the amygdala, lateral septum, nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex.
source: Consistent with previous reports, GFP-positive axon terminals were detected in the known targets of HPC, including the amygdala (Takahashi et al., 2005; Parfitt et al., 2017), lateral septum (Takahashi et al., 2005; Canteras and Swanson, 1992; Risold and Swanson, 1997; Parfitt et al., 2017, nucleus accumbens Amaral and Witter, 1989; Friedman et al., 2002) and prefrontal cortex (Parfitt et al., 2017; Amaral and Witter, 1989; Friedman et al., 2002) (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous reports and anterograde tracing data (though data not shown in manuscript).

claim: Within the hypothalamus, HPC axon terminals were found most abundantly in the AHN based on a normalized measure of GFP fluorescence intensity.
source: Within the hypothalamus, HPC axon terminals were found most abundantly in the AHN based on a normalized measure of GFP fluorescence intensity (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: Supported by quantified fluorescence intensity data from anterograde tracing (Figure 3b and c).

claim: The VMHdm/c and PMD were almost excluded from HPC innervation.
source: In stark contrast, the VMHdm/c and PMD, the other two main components of the medial hypothalamic defense system were almost excluded from the HPC innervation.
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data showing minimal HPC terminals in VMHdm/c and PMD (Figure 3b and c).

claim: The hippocampal innervation of the AHN showed an overall bias against other medial hypothalamic nuclei implicated in stress-induced corticosterone release (PVN) and social aggression (VMHvl).
source: Furthermore, the hippocampal innervation of the AHN showed an overall bias against other medial hypothalamic nuclei implicated in stress-induced corticosterone release (PVN) and social aggression (VMHvl) (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: Supported by quantified fluorescence intensity data comparing HPC innervation across hypothalamic nuclei (Figure 3b and c).

claim: The AHN is the primary entry point for HPC inputs to the medial hypothalamic defense system.
source: This data indicates that the AHN is the primary entry point for HPC inputs to the medial hypothalamic defense system.
evidence: Inferred from anterograde tracing data showing preferential HPC innervation of AHN compared to other components of the medial hypothalamic defense system.

claim: Photostimulation of HPC terminals triggered robust action potential firings of AHN cells in cell-attached voltage-clamp mode.
source: In the cell-attached voltage-clamp mode, photostimulation of HPC terminals (473 nm, 5ms pulses at 15 Hz) triggered robust action potential firings of AHN cells (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recording data (Figure 3e).

claim: Photostimulation of HPC terminals induced short-latency (average latency 3.6ms) excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) with average amplitude 132 pA in whole-cell voltage clamp mode.
source: In the whole-cell voltage clamp mode, photostimulation induced short-latency (average latency 3.6ms) excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) (average amplitude 132 pA; Figure 3f–h).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recording data (Figure 3f–h).

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs in the AHN were not affected by GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (PTX, 100 µM).
source: Light-evoked EPSCs in the AHN were not affected by GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (PTX, 100 µM) but eliminated by AMPA/kainite receptor antagonist DNQX (10 µM), indicating that HPC input to the AHN is glutamatergic in nature (Figure 3i and j).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recording data with pharmacological manipulations (Figure 3i and j).

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs in the AHN were eliminated by AMPA/kainite receptor antagonist DNQX (10 µM).
source: Light-evoked EPSCs in the AHN were not affected by GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (PTX, 100 µM) but eliminated by AMPA/kainite receptor antagonist DNQX (10 µM), indicating that HPC input to the AHN is glutamatergic in nature (Figure 3i and j).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recording data with pharmacological manipulations (Figure 3i and j).

claim: HPC input to the AHN is glutamatergic in nature.
source: Light-evoked EPSCs in the AHN were not affected by GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (PTX, 100 µM) but eliminated by AMPA/kainite receptor antagonist DNQX (10 µM), indicating that HPC input to the AHN is glutamatergic in nature (Figure 3i and j).
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological experiments showing DNQX sensitivity and PTX insensitivity of light-evoked EPSCs.

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs were eliminated by TTX (1 μM) but recovered after the application of 4-AP (100 μM), indicating monosynaptic transmission from ChR2-expressing HPC terminal boutons.
source: To isolate monosynaptic inputs from ChR2-expressing HPC axons, we sequentially added tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM) and 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 100 μM) to the ACSF. The previously observed light-evoked EPSCs were eliminated by TTX but recovered after the application of 4-AP, lending further support that monosynaptic transmission was triggered by direct ChR2-mediated depolarization of HPC terminal boutons (Hoover and Vertes, 2007, Figure 3k and l).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recording data with TTX and 4-AP application (Figure 3k and l).

claim: The AHN receives direct monosynaptic excitatory inputs from the HPC.
source: Together, our anterograde tracing and electrophysiological recording demonstrate that the AHN receives direct monosynaptic excitatory inputs from the HPC.
evidence: Supported by combined anterograde tracing and electrophysiological data showing anatomical connectivity and functional synaptic transmission.

claim: The AHN plays a specialized role in the medial hypothalamic defensive system, different from other major components, namely the PMD and VMHdm/c.
source: These findings also suggest that the AHN plays a specialized role in the medial hypothalamic defensive system, different from other major components, namely the PMD and VMHdm/c.
evidence: Inferred from the unique pattern of HPC innervation to AHN compared to PMD and VMHdm/c.

claim: Photostimulation of HPC axon terminals synapse on both GABA and glutamatergic cells in the AHN.
source: As expected, photostimulation evoked action potential spikes in mCherry-positive AHN GABA cells. However, we did not find any significant difference in the number of photostimulation-induced spikes between mCherry-positive and mCherry-negative cells, indicating that HPC axon terminals synapse on both GABA and glutamatergic cells in the AHN (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c-i).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recording data from mCherry-positive and mCherry-negative AHN cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c-i).

claim: Activation of HPC→AHN pathway produced light-synched, reversible increases in running bouts and speed.
source: To our surprise, the pathway activation did not elicit robust escape jumping or freezing observed in the direct AHN activation. Instead, it produced light-synched, reversible increases in running bouts and speed (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses to HPC→AHN pathway activation (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).

claim: Activation of HPC→AHN pathway did not elicit robust escape jumping or freezing observed in direct AHN activation.
source: To our surprise, the pathway activation did not elicit robust escape jumping or freezing observed in the direct AHN activation. Instead, it produced light-synched, reversible increases in running bouts and speed (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing behavioral responses between HPC→AHN pathway activation and direct AHN activation.

claim: Only grooming was decreased during the 6 Hz light stimulation of HPC→AHN pathway.
source: We also examined light-induced changes in consummatory (rearing, grooming) behaviors (Figure 4g and h, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and found that only grooming was decreased during the 6 Hz light stimulation (Figure 4f–h, Figure 4—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing changes in consummatory behaviors during pathway activation (Figure 4f–h, Figure 4—figure supplement 2f).

claim: Delivery of bursts of light pulses (20 Hz, 10 s ON, 10 s OFF) for 30 min during physical restraint significantly increased escape-associated struggle movements in ChR2 mice compared to controls.
source: To corroborate the effects of activating HPC→AHN pathway on escape-associated locomotion, we repeated the same pathway activation during physical restraint condition. The delivery of bursts of light pulses (20 Hz, 10 s ON, 10 s OFF) for 30 min significantly increased escape-associated struggle movements in ChR2 mice compared to controls (Figure 4i), consistent with the effect of direct AHN soma activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing struggle movements during physical restraint with pathway activation (Figure 4i).

claim: HPC→AHN pathway activity promotes escape responses by inducing locomotion.
source: Thus, our data suggests that HPC→AHN pathway activity promotes escape responses by inducing locomotion.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing increased locomotion and struggle movements during pathway activation.

claim: ChR2 mice gradually developed an avoidance to a chamber paired with light stimulation at both 6 Hz and 20 Hz frequency during the RTPA task.
source: During the subsequent RTPA task, ChR2 mice gradually developed an avoidance to a chamber paired with light stimulation at both 6 Hz and 20 Hz frequency (Figure 5e and f, Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing place avoidance during HPC→AHN pathway activation (Figure 5e and f).

claim: ChR2 mice that received HPC→AHN pathway stimulation during RTPA at 6 Hz displayed a robust conditioned aversion to the stimulation chamber.
source: One day after the RTPA task, mice were tested for memory retention in the CPA task. ChR2 mice that received HPC→AHN pathway stimulation during RTPA at 6 Hz, but not 20 Hz, displayed a robust conditioned aversion to the stimulation chamber (Figurer 5 h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing conditioned place aversion after 6 Hz pathway stimulation (Figure 5h).

claim: ChR2 mice that received HPC→AHN pathway stimulation during RTPA at 20 Hz did not display a robust conditioned aversion to the stimulation chamber.
source: One day after the RTPA task, mice were tested for memory retention in the CPA task. ChR2 mice that received HPC→AHN pathway stimulation during RTPA at 6 Hz, but not 20 Hz, displayed a robust conditioned aversion to the stimulation chamber (Figurer 5 h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lack of conditioned place aversion after 20 Hz pathway stimulation (Figure 5h).

claim: HPC→AHN pathway activity is aversive.
source: To evaluate whether the HPC→AHN pathway activity is intrinsically aversive and sufficient to induce a conditioned place aversion, we used the RTPA and CPA paradigms (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing real-time place avoidance during pathway activation.

claim: HPC→AHN pathway activity is sufficient to induce a conditioned place aversion.
source: To evaluate whether the HPC→AHN pathway activity is intrinsically aversive and sufficient to induce a conditioned place aversion, we used the RTPA and CPA paradigms (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing conditioned place aversion after pathway activation.

claim: L-Felinine is a putative predator kairomone of a Felidae species.
source: L-Felinine is a putative predator kairomone of a Felidae species (Voznessenskaya et al., 2016; Kvasha et al., 2018) and was chosen as a predator cue because it induces a robust dose-dependent increase in freezing compared to predator urine samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature and experimental data showing dose-dependent freezing response (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: L-Felinine induces a robust dose-dependent increase in freezing compared to predator urine samples.
source: L-Felinine is a putative predator kairomone of a Felidae species (Voznessenskaya et al., 2016; Kvasha et al., 2018) and was chosen as a predator cue because it induces a robust dose-dependent increase in freezing compared to predator urine samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing freezing responses to different concentrations of L-Felinine and predator urine (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: GFP control mice displayed an avoidance of the L-Felinine context during post-conditioning test.
source: As expected, GFP control mice displayed an avoidance of the L-Felinine context (Figure 6c and d, Figure 6—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing place avoidance in GFP control mice (Figure 6c and d, Figure 6—figure supplement 4a).

claim: ArchT mice failed to remember and avoid L-Felinine context during post-conditioning test.
source: ArchT mice, however, failed to remember and avoid L-Felinine context (Figure 6c and d, Figure 6—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lack of place avoidance in ArchT mice (Figure 6c and d, Figure 6—figure supplement 4b).

claim: The contextual memory impairment in ArchT mice was accompanied by significant decreases in defensive behavioral responses such as freezing, escape runs, and grooming compared to GFP control.
source: Furthermore, the contextual memory impairment was accompanied by significant decreases in defensive behavioral responses such as freezing, escape runs, and grooming compared to GFP control (Figure 6e–h, Video 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced defensive behaviors in ArchT mice (Figure 6e–h).

claim: c-Fos expression in ArchT mice was decreased in the AHN and PMD, but not in the VMHdm/c, compared to GFP control.
source: We found that c-Fos expression in ArchT mice was decreased in the AHN and PMD, but not in the VMHdm/c, compared to GFP control (Figure 6i and j).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data showing c-Fos expression levels (Figure 6i and j).

claim: The HPC→AHN pathway enables animals to avoid the environment associated with predators by driving AHN activities during the retrieval of contextual memory of predator cues.
source: Together, our data demonstrates that the HPC→AHN pathway enables animals to avoid the environment associated with predators by driving AHN activities during the retrieval of contextual memory of predator cues.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic inhibition experiments showing impaired contextual memory and reduced AHN activity.

claim: The pathway stimulation in ChR2 mice at both 6 and 20 Hz frequencies evoked goal-directed escapes toward the shelter, with a shorter latency to escape and a greater speed of escape running compared to GFP controls.
source: The pathway stimulation in ChR2 mice at both frequencies evoked goal-directed escapes toward the shelter, with a shorter latency to escape and a greater speed of escape running compared to GFP controls (Figure 7f–i, Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing escape latency and speed during pathway activation (Figure 7f–i).

claim: The behavioral response evoked by HPC→AHN pathway activation is not just a simple increase in locomotion but constitutes a goal-directed escape toward a safe shelter.
source: Thus, our findings show that the behavioral response evoked by HPC→AHN pathway activation is not just a simple increase in locomotion but constitutes a goal-directed escape toward a safe shelter.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing directed escape to shelter during pathway activation.

claim: Ultrasound stimuli (17–22 kHz) evoke strong defensive responses in mice, including escape flight and freezing.
source: Like predator odors, highfrequency (17–22 kHz) ultrasound stimuli evoke strong defensive responses in mice, including escape flight and freezing (Wöhr and Schwarting, 2010; Fendt et al., 2018; Sales, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ultrasound-evoked defensive responses.

claim: The same ultrasound stimulus elicits different defensive responses depending on the availability of a safe shelter; mice display escape flights when a safe shelter is available but freezing when there is no shelter.
source: A recent study found that the same ultrasound stimulus elicits different defensive responses depending on the availability of a safe shelter; mice display escape flights when a safe shelter is available but freezing when there is no shelter (Vale et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study demonstrating context-dependent defensive responses.

claim: Animals' spatial knowledge about escape routes and shelter availability determines the best course of defensive actions in the face of predatory threats.
source: The study suggests that animals' spatial knowledge about escape routes and shelter availability determines the best course of defensive actions in the face of predatory threats.
evidence: Inferred from cited study showing context-dependent defensive responses.

claim: Upon hearing the ultrasound threat, mice first turned its heads towards the shelter and initiated an escape flight, reaching a maximum running speed at the middle of the escape path.
source: Upon hearing the ultrasound threat, mice first turned its heads towards the shelter and initiated an escape flight, reaching a maximum running speed at the middle of the escape path, which are the known features of the goal-directed escape flight (Figure 8e, shelter, Figure 8—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing escape trajectory and speed profile (Figure 8e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1a-c).

claim: When the shelter was removed from the maze before the survey stage, the ultrasound threat failed to elicit escape flights, but instead caused either freezing or slow and disorganized flights in random directions.
source: Consistent with a previous report, mice displayed these characteristic escape responses only when a shelter is available. When the shelter was removed from the maze before the survey stage, the ultrasound threat failed to elicit escape flights, but instead caused either freezing or slow and disorganized flights in random directions (Figure 8e, no shelter, Figure 8—figure supplement 1d-h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses without shelter (Figure 8e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1d-h).

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of the HPC→AHN pathway produced disorganized escape trajectories and slow escape running speed in ArchT mice.
source: Optogenetic inhibition of the HPC→AHN pathway produced a range of effects on the goal-directed escape. Instead of a quick and direct flight to shelter seen in GFP controls, ArchT mice displayed disorganized escape trajectories and slow escape running speed, reminiscent of how the control mice respond to ultrasound when the shelter is not available (Figure 8f, Figure 8—figure supplement 2a,b, Video 9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing escape trajectories and speed during pathway inhibition (Figure 8f, Figure 8—figure supplement 2a,b).

claim: ArchT mice directed their flights to locations farther away from the target shelter (lower escape accuracy).
source: In addition, ArchT mice directed their flights to locations farther away from the target shelter (i.e. lower escape accuracy, Figure 8g), resulting in low escape success rate of 30% (6 out of 20 trials) compared to 87% in GFP controls (13 out of 15 trials) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2c,d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing escape accuracy during pathway inhibition (Figure 8g).

claim: ArchT mice had a low escape success rate of 30% (6 out of 20 trials) compared to 87% in GFP controls (13 out of 15 trials).
source: In addition, ArchT mice directed their flights to locations farther away from the target shelter (i.e. lower escape accuracy, Figure 8g), resulting in low escape success rate of 30% (6 out of 20 trials) compared to 87% in GFP controls (13 out of 15 trials) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2c,d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing escape success rates (Figure 8—figure supplement 2c,d).

claim: The lower escape accuracy and rate of successful escape suggest that ArchT mice failed to use a memory of shelter availability and shelter location to support their goal-directed escapes.
source: The lower escape accuracy and rate of successful escape suggest that ArchT mice failed to use a memory of shelter availability and shelter location to support their goal-directed escapes.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing impaired escape performance during pathway inhibition.

claim: A decrease in the organization and efficiency of escape was indicated by changes in various parameters such as escape linearity, escape duration, time to reach the maximum speed and increased freezing.
source: Furthermore, a decrease in the organization and efficiency of escape was indicated by changes in various parameters such as escape linearity, escape duration, time to reach the maximum speed and increased freezing (Figure 8h–k).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing multiple escape parameters during pathway inhibition (Figure 8h–k).

claim: The impairments in goal-directed escape were not accompanied with any changes in anxiety-related behaviors.
source: The impairments in goal-directed escape were not accompanied with any changes in anxiety-related behaviors (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no changes in anxiety-related behaviors (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).

claim: The inhibition of HPC→AHN pathway and removal of shelter significantly reduced c-Fos expression in the AHN compared to the control condition.
source: We found that the inhibition of HPC→AHN pathway and removal of shelter significantly reduced in the c-Fos measure in the AHN compared to the control condition (Control/Shelter+), whereas no change was detectable at the level of VMHdm/c and PMD (Figure 8l and m).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data showing c-Fos expression levels (Figure 8l and m).

claim: No change in c-Fos expression was detectable at the level of VMHdm/c and PMD when HPC→AHN pathway was inhibited or shelter was removed.
source: We found that the inhibition of HPC→AHN pathway and removal of shelter significantly reduced in the c-Fos measure in the AHN compared to the control condition (Control/Shelter+), whereas no change was detectable at the level of VMHdm/c and PMD (Figure 8l and m).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data showing c-Fos expression levels (Figure 8l and m).

claim: The AHN is not activated properly during the ultrasound-evoked escape if the HPC→AHN pathway is inhibited, or if a shelter is not available.
source: This suggests that the AHN is not activated properly during the ultrasound-evoked escape if the HPC→AHN pathway is inhibited, or if a shelter is not available.
evidence: Inferred from c-Fos data showing reduced AHN activity during pathway inhibition or without shelter.

claim: The inhibition of HPC→AHN pathway and the removal of shelter during the ultrasound-evoked escape produced similar effects at the behavioral level and on the AHN activity.
source: Thus, the inhibition of HPC→AHN pathway and the removal of shelter during the ultrasound-evoked escape produced similar effects not only at the behavioral level but also on the AHN activity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing similar behavioral and neural effects of pathway inhibition and shelter removal.

claim: The HPC→AHN pathway supports the goal-directed escape by driving the AHN activity with mnemonic information about shelter availability and shelter location.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the HPC→AHN pathway supports the goal-directed escape by driving the AHN activity with mnemonic information about shelter availability and shelter location.
evidence: Inferred from combined behavioral and neural data showing impaired escape and reduced AHN activity during pathway inhibition.

claim: The selective activation of excitatory VMHdm/c inputs to the AHN elicits escape running, immobility, and jumping.
source: This is consistent with a recent finding that the selective activation of excitatory VMHdm/c inputs to the AHN elicits escape running, immobility, and jumping (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study demonstrating the effects of VMHdm/c→AHN pathway activation.

claim: The selective activation of VMHdm/c inputs to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray produced only immobility but failed to evoke escape running and jumping.
source: Interestingly, however, the selective activation of VMHdm/c inputs to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray produced only immobility but failed to evoke escape running and jumping.
evidence: Stated as a fact, likely based on cited literature or established knowledge.

claim: Distinct aspects of defensive responses to threat are mediated by different cell types and efferent projections in the VMHdm/c and AHN.
source: These findings, together with ours, support the idea that distinct aspects of defensive responses to threat are mediated by different cell types and efferent projections in the VMHdm/c and AHN.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings and cited literature on pathway-specific defensive responses.

claim: The AHN is a largely GABAergic structure, with some scattered glutamatergic cells located at the ventral aspect of the medial zone.
source: The AHN has been shown to be a largely GABAergic structure, with some scattered glutamatergic cells located at the ventral aspect of the medial zone (Anagnostaras et al., 2001; Boudaba et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature describing the cellular composition of the AHN.

claim: Predatory context (e.g. cat-associated context) induces a robust increase in c-Fos level in the AHN.
source: Consistently, a previous work found that predatory context (e.g. cat-associated context) induces a robust increase in c-Fos level in the AHN (Cezario et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study showing c-Fos activation in AHN during predatory context exposure.

claim: The PMD, not the AHN, was identified as the most responsive hypothalamic region to predatory context despite the relative scarcity of hippocampal innervation in the PMD.
source: Interestingly, the same study identified the PMD, not the AHN, as the most responsive hypothalamic region to predatory context despite the relative scarcity of hippocampal innervation in the PMD.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study showing PMD activation during predatory context exposure.

claim: The PMD activation evokes an organized escape in which mice quickly assess environment's layout and find efficient flight path.
source: Furthermore, a recent study by Wang et al., 2021a found that the PMD activation evokes an organized escape in which mice quickly assess environment's layout and find efficient flight path, whereas the activation of other hypothalamic nuclei, including the AHN and VMHdm/c, only induced stereotyped panic-related escape responses such as running and jumping (Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study demonstrating the effects of PMD activation on escape behavior.

claim: The activation of AHN and VMHdm/c only induced stereotyped panic-related escape responses such as running and jumping.
source: Furthermore, a recent study by Wang et al., 2021a found that the PMD activation evokes an organized escape in which mice quickly assess environment's layout and find efficient flight path, whereas the activation of other hypothalamic nuclei, including the AHN and VMHdm/c, only induced stereotyped panic-related escape responses such as running and jumping (Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study demonstrating the effects of AHN and VMHdm/c activation on escape behavior.

claim: Once a shelter was added and mice formed a memory of shelter availability during the habituation stage, AHN activation evoked an organized goal-directed escape to shelter, instead of jumping and running.
source: However, once a shelter was added and mice formed a memory of shelter availability during the habituation stage, the same AHN activation evoked an organized goal-directed escape to shelter, instead of jumping and running.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing goal-directed escape to shelter during AHN activation after habituation.

claim: The VMHdm/c receives direct inputs from the medial and basolateral amygdala areas that process multimodal sensory information about predatory threat.
source: Despite not being strongly innervated by the hippocampus, the VMHdm/c receives direct inputs from the medial and basolateral amygdala areas that process multimodal sensory information about predatory threat.
evidence: Stated as a fact, likely based on established knowledge or cited literature.

claim: The VMHdm/c is activated earlier as mice approach a predatory threat, suggesting that its firing rate likely encode sensory aspects of threat intensity and threat distance.
source: Consistently, single-unit recordings showed that the VMHdm/c is activated earlier as mice approach a predatory threat, suggesting that its firing rate likely encode sensory aspects of threat intensity and threat distance (Esteban Masferrer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study showing VMHdm/c activation patterns during threat approach.

claim: Aversive experience such as the predator odor can induce remapping of place cell firing which becomes stabilized after 24 hr.
source: Aversive experience such as the predator odor can induce remapping of place cell firing which becomes stabilized after 24 hr.
evidence: Stated as a fact, likely based on established knowledge.

claim: HPC→AHN pathway is likely activated by a specific hippocampal place cell ensemble that represents predator odor location and context.
source: Thus, HPC→AHN pathway is likely activated by a specific hippocampal place cell ensemble that represents predator odor location and context.
evidence: Speculative inference based on known hippocampal place cell function and experimental findings.

claim: Mice can make accurate escape flights even in complete darkness, suggesting that external landmarks (reference memory) are not required for mice to determine the shelter location.
source: Importantly, a previous study using the same assay has shown that unlike in Morris water maze or Barnes maze tests, mice can make accurate escape flights even in complete darkness, suggesting that external landmarks (reference memory) are not required for mice to determine the shelter location.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study demonstrating escape behavior in darkness.

claim: Mice compute an escape vector to the shelter location by integrating self-motion over time using the path integration strategy.
source: Instead, mice compute an escape vector to the shelter location by integrating self-motion over time using the path integration strategy (Vale et al., 2017; Vale et al., 2020; Bang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating path integration during escape behavior.

claim: The retrosplenial cortex (RSP) input to superior colliculus (SC) plays an important role in shelter-directed escape by continuously encoding egocentric representation of shelter direction.
source: A recent study found that the retrosplenial cortex (RSP) input to superior colliculus (SC) plays an important role in shelter-directed escape by continuously encoding egocentric representation of shelter direction (Vale et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study demonstrating the role of RSP-SC pathway in escape behavior.

claim: The HPC-AHN pathway controls the motivational drive to escape based on shelter availability while the RSP-SC pathway controls the escape direction based on shelter location.
source: It is plausible that the HPC-AHN pathway controls the motivational drive to escape based on shelter availability while the RSP-SC pathway controls the escape direction based on shelter location.
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental findings and cited literature.
